Take with food to improve tolerability

summary: Evening primrose oil (EPO) is a dietary supplement extracted from Oenothera biennis seeds, rich in the omega-6 fatty acid gamma-linolenic acid (GLA). It is taken by mouth, typically 1-4 g/day, and is used by the public for atopic eczema, cyclical mastalgia, premenstrual symptoms and other conditions, though robust efficacy evidence is limited. It is not FDA-approved as a drug. It is generally well tolerated; main concerns are mild GI upset, a possible increased bleeding tendency, and rare reports of lowered seizure threshold.
indications: Used traditionally/by self-care for atopic eczema and skin dryness (efficacy not established)
Cyclical and non-cyclical mastalgia (breast pain) - historical use
Premenstrual syndrome symptoms - popular use, limited evidence
Menopausal hot flushes and rheumatoid arthritis symptoms - investigational/unproven

dosage.d: 1-4 g/day of evening primrose oil orally (providing ~80-320 mg GLA)
dosage.n: Doses are not standardized; follow product label

dosage.d: Commonly 2-6 g/day in adults; lower in children, in divided doses
dosage.n: Evidence does not consistently support benefit
Effect may take 8-12 weeks; benefit uncertain

dosage.d: Lower weight-appropriate amounts per product label

admin: Take oral capsules with food to reduce stomach upset
Use a consistent daily schedule; effects on conditions like mastalgia may take weeks to months
Discontinue 1-2 weeks before elective surgery due to possible bleeding risk
Store away from heat and light to prevent rancidity of the oil
moa: Evening primrose oil supplies gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), an omega-6 fatty acid that is metabolized to dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid and onward to series-1 prostaglandins (e.g., PGE1) and other eicosanoids. These mediators are proposed to exert anti-inflammatory effects and to support skin barrier lipids, the putative basis for its traditional uses.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to evening primrose oil or its components
relative: Bleeding disorders or use of anticoagulant/antiplatelet drugs
Seizure disorder or use of seizure-threshold-lowering drugs (e.g., phenothiazines)

preg: There are insufficient data on safety in pregnancy and some concern about effects on labor; avoid use during pregnancy, particularly near term, unless advised by a clinician.
lact: Limited data are available on use during breastfeeding. Small amounts of GLA appear in milk; use cautiously and only if needed.
renal: No specific data in renal impairment; use with general caution as with any supplement.
hepatic: No specific data in hepatic impairment; use with general caution.

major: Anticoagulants/antiplatelets (warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel) - possible additive bleeding risk
moderate: Phenothiazines and other agents that lower seizure threshold - possible increased seizure risk
Anti-seizure medications - theoretical reduction in effect
minor: Other herbal products with antiplatelet effects (ginkgo, garlic, fish oil) - additive bleeding tendency
interactions.food: Take with food; no specific food to avoid.
interactions.alcohol: No specific documented interaction with alcohol.
interactions.diagnostics: May modestly affect bleeding/coagulation parameters; no characteristic lab interference.

monitoring: Signs of bruising or bleeding, particularly with anticoagulants/antiplatelets
Seizure frequency in patients with epilepsy
Symptom response for the targeted condition
counsel: This is a dietary supplement, not an FDA-approved medicine; tell your doctor you are taking it
Take with food to avoid stomach upset
Stop and inform your surgeon about 2 weeks before any operation
Tell your doctor if you take blood thinners or have a seizure disorder
Benefits for conditions like breast pain may take 2-3 months to appear, if any
pk: Gradual; clinical effects (if any) over weeks
GLA absorbed and incorporated into lipids over hours to days
Not formally characterized for the supplement
Store in a cool, dry place away from light; refrigeration prevents rancidity
pearls: NOT FDA-approved as a drug - this record is based on monograph/herbal references (BNF/EMA herbal and supplement literature) and traditional use, not an FDA label
Main active component is gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), an omega-6 fatty acid
Evidence for atopic eczema and mastalgia is weak/inconsistent in controlled trials
Theoretical bleeding risk - stop before surgery and use caution with anticoagulants
Avoid co-use with phenothiazines because of possible lowered seizure threshold
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose. Do not take a double dose. Missing an occasional dose of a supplement is not harmful.
overdose: Acute overdose is unlikely to be dangerous; excessive intake may cause loose stools, nausea and abdominal discomfort. Management is supportive. Watch for bleeding in patients also taking anticoagulants.
